The peritoneum also contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic tissue, which help to supply the organs within the abdomen with oxygen and nutrients, and remove waste products.

The structure of the peritoneum varies depending on the location within the body. In the abdomen, the parietal layer is continuous with the diaphragm, while in the pelvis, the parietal layer is divided into separate sections by the pelvic brim.

The visceral layer of the peritoneum is highly vascularized and contains many blood vessels, which help to provide oxygen and nutrients to the organs within the abdomen.

The peritoneum also plays a role in the immune system, as it contains lymphoid tissue and macrophages, which help to fight off infections and cancer cells.

This is mediated by selectins, which are adhesion molecules that interact with carbohydrates on the surface of neutrophils (and other leukocytes) called sialyl Lewis X (sLeX). When a neutrophil contacts the vascular wall, it rolls along the vascular wall until it reaches a region where there is an increased concentration of chemoattractants or a low pH. At this point, the neutrophil becomes activated and begins to bind to the vascular wall via integrins. These interactions between integrins and extracellular matrix components result in firm attachment of the neutrophil to the vascular wall. Finally, once attached, neutrophils undergo transmigration through the vascular wall into surrounding tissue.
